lead: A class is only a plan; the objects made from it need a starting state. Python gives every class a special method, __init__, that runs automatically the moment an object is created, so attributes such as a balance or a roll number are never missing. A second special method, __del__, runs when the object is about to be removed. Inside both, the parameter self holds the particular object being worked on. These three pieces — creation, the self link, and destruction — explain why an object behaves like a small self-contained machine, and they appear in every Python library you will read.
prereq: You need: 4.1 Classes and objects and Unit 2 (functions, arguments and default values).

sections.h3: __init__: the initializer that runs on creation

blocks.text: c1 = Counter(5) does two jobs. Python first builds a blank object of the class — that step is __new__, and you almost never write it. Then Python calls Counter.__init__(c1, 5). The code inside __init__ runs before the assignment finishes, so c1 is never a half-built object with missing attributes.

The usual shape is def __init__(self, n): self.n = n. __init__ is the initializer: a special method whose name carries two underscores on each side (a dunder name), which Python calls for you. Some syllabi call it the constructor. Strictly, Python splits the work — __new__ creates, __init__ initialises — but the split matters only in rare cases such as subclassing immutable types.

Parameters work as in any function. Defaults are common: def __init__(self, name, balance=0) lets you write Account("Ravi") and get a zero balance. A default value is computed once, when the class body runs, not once per object. So a mutable default such as items=[] is shared by every object of that class. Write items=None and set self.items = [] inside the method.

__init__ must return None. A bare return, or no return at all, is fine. Writing return self.n raises TypeError: __init__() should return None, not 'int' at the moment of creation. Otherwise it is an ordinary method: c1.__init__(9) runs it a second time and overwrites attributes.

sections.h3: self: the object's handle inside the method

blocks.text: When you write c1.deposit(100), Python really runs Counter.deposit(c1, 100). The object itself is pushed in as the first argument, so the parameter named self receives it. That is the whole meaning of self: the object on which the method was called.
self is not a keyword. Any name works and the program still runs. Every Python programmer writes self, so you should too.

Leaving it out is the classic mistake. def deposit(amount): inside the class gives TypeError: deposit() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given when you call c1.deposit(100) — the call passes two values (the object and 100) while the definition accepts one.

Two objects keep two separate states. After c1 = Counter(5) and c2 = Counter(7), the attribute c1.n is 5 and c2.n is 7; inside the method, self is whichever object came in. Use self.attr for the object's own attribute, Counter.count for a shared class variable, and self.method() to call a sibling method. Nothing is hidden, so you always see which object is being changed.

sections.h3: Object lifetime: reference counting, __del__ and del

blocks.text: An object lives from creation until the last reference to it disappears. A reference is a name or container slot pointing at it: c1, a list element, a function argument. CPython counts them; sys.getrefcount(c1) reports the count, one higher than you expect because the argument itself is a reference.

When the count reaches zero, Python calls __del__(self), the destructor, once, and then frees the memory. An object trapped in a reference cycle that nothing outside points to is left to the garbage collector, which also runs __del__ — later, and in an order you did not choose.

del c1 removes the name, not the object. If b = c1 still exists, no destructor runs; the object survives until b goes too. In the example below, del c1 drops the only reference, so __del__ fires at that exact line.

The timing of __del__ is therefore not fixed. It may run at interpreter shutdown, after your last print, possibly in an unexpected order. It is a fine place to decrement a counter or write a log line. It is a poor place to close a file or release a lock: use with or try/finally instead (see Unit 5, Exceptions, Files and Modules).

figure.caption: Creating c1 and c2 raises the class counter to 2; del c1 removes the only reference to the first object, so its destructor runs and the count falls to 1, which the last print shows.

spec.title: Object lifetime
spec.aria: Creating c1 calls __init__ and sets count to 1; creating c2 sets count to 2; del c1 calls __del__, lowers count to 1 and the final print shows 1.

examples.question: Define a class Counter with a class variable count = 0. The method __init__(self, n) stores n in self.n and adds 1 to Counter.count. The method __del__(self) subtracts 1 from Counter.count and prints the word bye followed by self.n. Write the statements c1 = Counter(5); c2 = Counter(7); print(Counter.count); del c1; print(Counter.count). Give the exact output, in order.
steps: The class body runs first: Counter.count becomes 0 and the two methods are defined. No object exists yet.
c1 = Counter(5): the object is created, __init__ receives self = c1 and n = 5, so c1.n = 5 and Counter.count becomes 1.
c2 = Counter(7): c2.n = 7 and Counter.count becomes 2.
del c1 removes the name c1. That was the only reference to the first object, so its reference count reaches 0, __del__ runs, prints bye 5, and Counter.count becomes 2 - 1 = 1.
del c2 removes the last reference to the second object, so __del__ runs at that line, prints bye 7, and Counter.count becomes 1 - 1 = 0. Nothing is left to interpreter shutdown.
Output in order: 2, bye 5, 1, bye 7. The first print shows count 2; del c1 prints bye 5 and drops count to 1; the second print shows 1; del c2 prints bye 7 and drops count to 0 (0 is not printed).
examples.check:
class Counter:
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        Counter.count += 1

    def __del__(self):
        Counter.count -= 1


c1 = Counter(5)
c2 = Counter(7)
print(Counter.count)
del c1
print(Counter.count)

code.code:
class Counter:
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        Counter.count += 1

    def __del__(self):
        Counter.count -= 1
        print("bye", self.n)


c1 = Counter(5)
c2 = Counter(7)
print(Counter.count)
del c1
print(Counter.count)
del c2   # release the last object now, so its destructor does not wait for shutdown

traps: Treating __del__ as guaranteed cleanup. Its timing is not fixed, it may run at interpreter shutdown, and it is unsafe for closing files or releasing locks.
Saying __init__ creates the object. __new__ creates it; __init__ only fills in attributes, and it must return None.
Confusing del c1 with destruction. del removes one name; the object dies only when its reference count reaches zero.
Forgetting self in a method definition, then misreading the error TypeError: method() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given.
Using a mutable default in __init__, such as items=[]. One list is created once and shared by every object of the class.

quiz.a: None. A bare return or no return statement is correct; returning any other value raises TypeError when the object is created.

quiz.q: What does the statement del c1 actually do?
quiz.a: It removes the name c1 from the current scope. The object is destroyed only if no other reference to it remains; then __del__ runs and the memory is freed.

quiz.q: Why does every instance method take self as its first parameter?
quiz.a: Because the call c1.deposit(100) is executed as Counter.deposit(c1, 100): Python passes the object itself as the first argument. self is the name that receives it, which is how the method body reaches that object's attributes.

quiz.q:
Give the output:
class Box:
    def __init__(self, w, h=2):
        self.w = w
        self.h = h

b1 = Box(3)
b2 = Box(4, 5)
print(b1.w * b1.h, b2.w * b2.h)
quiz.a: b1 takes the default h = 2, so b1.w * b1.h = 3 × 2 = 6. b2 passes h = 5, so 4 × 5 = 20. Output: 6 20

quiz.q:
Give the output and explain it:
class Bag:
    def __init__(self, items=[]):
        self.items = items

a = Bag()
b = Bag()
a.items.append("rice")
print(b.items)
quiz.a: Output: ['rice']. The default list is built once, when the class body runs, so a.items and b.items are the same list object. The fix is items=None, then self.items = [] inside __init__.

quiz.q:
Give the output and justify each line:
class T:
    def __del__(self):
        print("gone")

a = T()
b = a
del a
print("still here")
del b
quiz.a: Output: still here, then gone. After b = a the object has two references, so del a leaves the count at 1 and no destructor runs. print outputs still here. del b drops the last reference, the count reaches 0, and __del__ prints gone.

quiz.q: A student writes file closing inside __del__ so that it happens automatically. Give two reasons the examiner would mark this wrong.
quiz.a: First, the timing is not fixed: __del__ may run long after the file is no longer needed, or at interpreter shutdown when other names are already being torn down. Second, if the object stays referenced (a list, a cycle, a global), __del__ may never run during the program, so the file stays open. Use with or try/finally instead.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production Python code rarely writes __del__; it uses context managers (with blocks) or weakref.finalize so cleanup happens at a predictable line. The __slots__ attribute on a class removes the per-object dictionary and shrinks memory when you create millions of small objects. Dataclasses generate __init__, __repr__ and comparison methods from field declarations, which is why modern application code writes far fewer initializers by hand. Search next for the Python data model (__new__ versus __init__), weakref, contextlib, and dataclasses.
